newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian investment seen below govt f'cast.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian investment seen below govt f'cast.

text.p: Australian business investment, one of the key factors underpinning growth, will not be as strong in fiscal 1996/97 (July/June) as the government forecast in the budget last month, economists believe.

Business investment growth will come in under the 14 percent the government has forecast and that will have flow-through effects to other areas of the economy and on the pace of economic growth, they said.

A Reuter survey of 31 economists, taken last Friday, found a median forecast of a 10.0 percent rise in investment in 1996/97. Forecasts ranged from a 7.0 percent rise to an 18.0 percent rise. Only three of those surveyed saw business investment as being stronger than the government forecast, with a further three expecting the investment in line with the forecast.
The Reserve Bank of Australia sees business investment as underpinning the government's 3.5 percent GDP growth forecast.
"The main key to achieving the 3.5 percent GDP growth forecast for 1996/97 is business investment," the then RBA Governor Bernie Fraser said in Tokyo earlier this month.
In line with this outlook, those who forecast investment at under 14 percent tended to have softer growth forecasts as well.

"Well it obviously means that the government's growth forecast of 3.5 percent for the fiscal year, will be not achieved, and given that we're more pessimistic on the outlook for private consumption, there's a good chance that growth will come in under three percent," Merrill Lynch Australia chief economist Nigel Douglas said of his 11 percent forecast.

Economists said a key factor behind the softer forecast was that the business environment had changed markedly in 1996, and that some of the euphoria surrounding the election of the conservative coalition government in March has died down.

"I think it's worth remembering that when the government put together their forecasts for business investment for 1996/97, they had the capital expenditure survey, and that pointed to very strong growth," Citibank Australia senior economist Stephen Koukoulas said.

"Now part of that was linked, I think, to some of the post election euphoria ... but since then we've seen some of the other business sentiment surveys just come off the boil a little bit so perhaps some of those expectations won't be realised," he said.

The official capital expenditure survey allows projections to be drawn from business investment intentions through the use of realisation ratios, which equate previous survey estimates to actual outcomes.
While the previous ratios suggested strong growth in 1996/97, the greater than expected slowing of the economy this year may render the comparision invalid, economists said.
An interest rate cut was delivered on July 31, against the expectations of many, as the RBA sought to boost the pace of activity to make inroads into unemployment.
With many areas of the economy still sluggish, the flow-through effect to profits and earnings may mean companies are reluctant to commit to big investment projects, they said.

"Because we expect the outlook for company profits to deteriorate over the year, we expect a lower realisation ratio for 1996/97 than in 1995/96," Westpac's general manager of economics, Bill Evans said.
Evans added that this view meant the necessary realisation ratio to achive the government forecast looked too optimistic.
